claim.why_it_matters: The sub-items of general rule 5 are detached from their parent and sit flush left immediately above the top-level '6)', so they read as peers of the numbered general rules rather than as the two conditions that apply when SEPARATE CHARACTER is NOT specified - the exact opposite condition to rule 6 that follows them. The inconsistency is visible within the same page slice, since rule 6's identical a)/b) pair IS indented.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED - whitespace-only, and not even a page-514-specific anomaly. 1. The claim's description of both sources is literally accurate but describes nothing more than leading spaces. I rendered p514 at 300 dpi (E:/Temp/specrecon/v514/spec_p514.png, printed folio 484) and read specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 21672-21692. Every word of the page is present in the markdown, verbatim, in the printed reading order: rule 5's stem ('5) If the SEPARATE CHARACTER phrase is not specified, then:', line 21672, foot of p513), then a), then b), then 6), then its a) and b), then 7). Nothing is missing, added, reordered, or misquoted - including the en-dash glyph in 6b's "'+' and '-'". The ONLY delta between PDF and markdown on this page is three leading space characters on two lines. 2. 'misplaced-content' is the wrong label: nothing is misplaced. The two sub-items sit exactly where the PDF puts them - after rule 5's colon and before rule 6. They cannot be misread as peers of the numbered general rules because they carry LETTER markers (a/b), not numbers, and the numbered sequence 4) 5) 6) 7) is intact and unbroken around them; and they cannot be misattached to rule 6 because they precede it. The nesting is recoverable from the marker style and position alone, so meaning is unaffected. 3. The premise that this is a page-514 defect is false - it is the transcription's document-wide whitespace convention. specs/ISO_COBOL.md contains 572 flush-left '^[a-z]) ' sub-items versus 777 three-space-indented ones. Only 105 of the flush-left ones follow a page header, so this is not even primarily a page-break artifact: e.g. line 9178 '2) When the value of operand-2 is greater than zero, the results shall be determined as follows:' is followed at line 9180 by a flush-left 'a)', mid-page, no page boundary in sight. Ledgering p514 for it would mean ledgering ~572 sites for the same cosmetic inconsistency. 4. What local page-boundary influence exists is ordinary page-break furniture, which reconciliation accepts by convention: rule 5's stem is separated from its sub-items by '---', '', '## Page 514' and the running header '# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)' (lines 21674-21681). That furniture is a far larger structural interruption than three spaces, and it is the agreed transcription format, not a discrepancy. The lost indent is a by-product of the same slice boundary. Per the rejection criteria - difference is only formatting / page-break furniture, and does not change meaning - real=false.
verdict.corrected_description: No content discrepancy. Page 514 is transcribed completely and faithfully; the sole difference is that general rule 5's two lettered sub-items lack the 3-space indent that rule 6's sub-items carry. That is leading whitespace only, it is a document-wide inconsistency in the transcription (572 flush-left vs 777 indented lettered sub-items, most of them nowhere near a page break, e.g. line 9180), and the parent/child relationship remains unambiguous from the letter markers and the intact 4)/5)/6)/7) numbering. If it is ever worth addressing, it is a single global normalization pass over the whole file, not a page-514 ledger entry.
